segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: He, was he a preacher?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: He was a preacher. And he used to preach.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you learn some of these songs from him?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah. In church.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, why don't you sing? Sing one for me.

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: And you going to catch it? Where are they? Ready?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Yeah. We're ready. Just go ahead.

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Is that alright? (sings)

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That's very nice… what is that?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: That's When the Roll is Called Up.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, when the roll is called? What do the words mean? End it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yes… that means when that man comes and sins, preacher… lord.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What does it mean to that? What have you said so far?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: When the roll is called up, there will be no more living… oh, okay.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What comes next?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Then next is they call them people across, and then they call them from there. That's the way it is.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know any others? Songs?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: The Lord is with you. The Lord is with you. The Lord is with you. The Lord is with you. Oh, they create with me. Can you catch that?

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What does that one mean?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: That's, uh, don't let the cross.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That's what?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Down at the cross. Down at the cross.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Who wrote the Nez Perce words for these? A lot of these are hymns in English, too, aren't they?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know who wrote the Nez Perce words for them?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I don't know. I can't tell you that. See, we used to be Catholic first, but I don't know what kind of trouble they had, so I go to Church of God now. You know Church of God? Church? That's what I go to now.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When you saw, when you used to see Father Cataldo, did he used to sing in Nez Perce, too?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Oh, just what we learned him. But they didn't sing very good. They used to make me start sing first.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: They used to make you start first?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh -huh. That's the way they do now, not the Church of God. They make me sing.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What other songs do you sing?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Oh, I've got quite a few songs. This is another one. (sings).

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What's that one called?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: When the Rulers Call Up Yonder.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh! That's the same one you sang the first time I think. Did they teach you songs like Rock of Ages and things like that in this verse?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What else did they teach you?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Jesus Christ, the Lord of the heavens, He gave His hand to the Lord, and He gave His hand to my Lord,… and He gave His hand to my Lord, and He gave His hand to my Lord,… and He gave His hand to my Lord, and He gave His hand to my Lord,… and we quit. My husband quit, so we both quit. His name was Paul Jackson.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Paul Jackson was your husband?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh huh… he died. My father's name was Lan Henry.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Lan Henry?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: And he died. And my mother's name was Agnes.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was her Nez Perce name? Whose?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Your mother's.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was her name?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: It's been so long.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What were the early days like when you were just a child? What was it like? Was the tribe on the reservation all the time then?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We used to always have church. When I got married with Paul, we'd come to Catholic church. But I don't know what happened to him, and he quit. Well, what about when... And he quit with Church of God Church.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: In the early days with the tribe, when you were young, did the men still do a lot of hunting, and did you still go gathering camas and everything?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, uh huh… they used to get camas, and they used to go out hunting. They'd have deer meat, and you'd have dry deer meat and eat that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of houses did you live in then? No. No, when you were a little girl.

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We had a tepee.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Mm hmm… but when we had that tepee, then my grandfather... My father went and got one father that can build a house. So he built a house. He built a pretty good house, and Daddy helped him. See, Daddy was a white man. Mm hmm. Uh huh. And he helped him, and so when he got through, he was upstairs to it… mm hmm… now, my son's living in that house now.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Where would you go to gather camas? Would you pack up the tepee and take it with you when you went to gather camas and everything?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: A long time ago. Yeah, a long time ago. Yeah, we used to take the tepee with us.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Where would you go?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Any place up in the mountains, hunting or something like that. They used to go. My husband used to be a great hunter.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: With a rifle?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah… we had to wash the rifle already. Uh huh. Uh huh. I used to dry meat. Oh, that dry meat's good.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How would you dry the meat?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, you just take it and take a knife and cut it if it's about this size. And cut it and open it this way and open it this way.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Does it kind of make little strips out of it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, not strips. Wide ones. About this wide.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: About a foot wide or something?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, about this long. Uh huh. And you put it on there. We used to dry it on the smoke… uh huh… we used to build a fire underneath.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long would it take to dry it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Oh, it took not too long to dry it. See, fire… smoke. Uh huh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you used to tan the hides and everything too?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Mama used to tan the hides.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was that very hard to do?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: She used to tan the hide.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was it very hard to tan the hide?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: It's hard. See, you first gonna soak it… you soak it… when you get the deer meat, you just take it and get a knife and cut it and sew it. About this long. And then you take it and soak it. When you get soaked in it, then you can... Well, we have some kind of iron. Take that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, to scrape the fat?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Scrape it, yeah. Scrape it this way.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Up and down?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, yeah… that's what we used to do with the meat. I mean, skin.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Then what would you do with it? How would you make it so it was tanned?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, we used to get some kind of a... Well, it was when they used to hunt like that. We'd get the brains from the deer. And we'd mix that brains with a little water. And then we'd soak it in there.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And that tans it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: And then you take it and you... We used to take a stick and put it over a pole or something and turn it… dry it up… and we'd open it up.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, you'd twist the skin around the stick so it got real tight and all the water ran out?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No. Just a little bit.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, you just put it on the stick and let it hang?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Let it tanned down and the water would all go out, you know. And you can tanned it quickly. I know how to tanned it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And then would you make clothing and things out of it? Huh? Would you then make clothing?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, we used to have clothes out of the deer hide. Yeah. We used to make dresses and things like that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: I imagine they were pretty nice, weren't they?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We used to use them. When we have war dance or something, then we wear them.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When you have what kind of a dance?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: War dance. Oh, a war dance.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did the Nez Perce have war dances?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, they have. Huh. They used to have war dances.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What were they like? Oh, you mean the dresser?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No, the dances… oh, we used to dance, but I don't know how I can tell you how.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of songs? Do they sing songs at the war dances?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: See, the war dance, they go up and down.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would there be somebody playing a drum or something?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, they played a drum. They played a drum and then they wore a dance.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was there a song they sang?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know that song?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No, I'm just getting too old. Okay.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What other kind of dances did they have?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, they used to have ending dance. Well, that's people that used to send the kids out themselves. They'd get some kind of a dream or something from something, some kind of an animal or something. That animal would give them a song. That's what they used to sing.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did both the boys and the girls go out to have medicine dreams?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was that when you were young too?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, they sent me out too, up in the mountains.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How long did you stay?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We went going out to huckleberry. Oh. That's where they sent me out, just one night.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were you all by yourself?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh -huh… i learned my song and everything. Uh -huh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What animal or what being gave your songs to you?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, if it's deer or any kind of animal. If it's deer or elk or sheep or anything.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What animal gave you yours? Or can't you tell me that?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Mine was a deer.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: It's a deer?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh -huh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you remember the song of the deer?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I used to sing it, but I don't sing it no more. I used to sing it when we used to have dance.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What would happen when you came back from the mountain with your song? What would you do then? Would there be a dance or something then when you got back?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No… a dance at wintertime. We used to dance at wintertime. Mama used to dance and grandma used to dance and grandfather and me. The boys never danced. I had three brothers and one sister, but she never went anywhere.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would there be big dances with a lot of people there? Would there be big dances?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We used to have long tent beds like this. The tent poles would be just like that. Oh, I see. No horn tent. Real long. With the poles locking together. Uh -huh. We used to have dancing there.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would there be a lot of people there?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, there used to be lots of people come to dance. Well, see, lots of old people, the ones that's old, they have some kind of a... they learn some kind of a doctrine.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Some kind of a what?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Doctor.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: A doctrine?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, they doctor a person that's sick. Yeah. Grandfather was like that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was he?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah. What...

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How would he do that? What kind of things would he do to doctor somebody?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, they sing, but when they're dancing, they talk. Uh -huh. But when they're taking care of the sick people, they just sing. And they just blow on it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Blow on the person?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh -huh. Blow on the person. Uh -huh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did they use plants and things, too, to help doctor with?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No. They just... Like that. Uh -huh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And how did that help?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: They used to help him quite a bit.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How did it help?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: See, first when he's going to doctor, then he talk. Talk his dream, what he did about them songs. Oh. And then he talk about that. When they get through, then they can blow on to you. Oh, I see.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And he would get his power?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Through that dream?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: And then he can take your head this way and..… oh… heave you up. Uh -huh… yeah… he used to... My grandfather was like that. He used to doctor. And he used to doctor even pretty sick people. Mm -hmm. Who gave him well. Mm -hmm. Uh -huh. That's the way that lives… what...

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When you were a girl in Nez Perce, did the tribe move around quite a bit?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I wish they were out in the mountains. Mm -hmm. Get their meat. We killed them and we dry it. We used to have dry meat. Mm -hmm.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What would you eat all winter? You'd eat the dry meat and what else?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, we could eat dry meat or else the boys would go out and hunt again. Uh -huh. Well... Their meat's pretty good. Oh, yes. Uh -huh. Yeah, their meat's pretty good.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, would you eat the camas too?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: They cook camas, cous.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: cous?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Is that the way the Nez Perce camas?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah… camas is different and cous is different. When they cook camas, it turns black… uh -huh… when they cook cous, they don't cook it under the ground, but this other one, they could cook it under the ground. Oh. And this other one, they don't. They just dry it up, just take the top off and dry it up, wash it clean and dry it up.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What does cous look like?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: White. They're white then.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: They have a white flower?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah. Uh -huh… kind of a pretty yellow. Uh -huh. They grow all over the hillsides.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, how would you dig camas?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, we used to have digger.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did that look like?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Tukas, we call it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: A what?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: About this long -- iron.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did you call it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Tukas. Tukas. And just about like this. Uh -huh. Tukas.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: A little bit of a bend?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, my mama used to put a piece of wood, clean it good and put that under like this.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, on the end of the tukas?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, they used to make a hole in that thing and put it on the tukas… oh, I see.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And then you just dig that under the plant?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, and dig the house out and tell us. Uh -huh.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Well, how would you make the camas so it wouldn't spoil?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, it is the same, but see, we have to cook it first. We used to do that. Hooks used to do that. Mama, they dig a ground.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Dig a big hole in the ground?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: They dig a big hole in the ground about this deep. About a couple, three feet deep. They put wood on top of it like this. Overlapping pieces of wood. Uh -huh. And then they put rocks on top of it. On top of it. Then they burn that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The camas would be under the wood?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No… it's going to be on top. Oh, I see. And then when they burn that wood, they fall, you know. And they take all the pieces of wood out. Just have a hot rock. Yeah, they take rocks and put it on top. That rocks get hot. They fall in. Then they dig grass. And they kind of sprinkle the rock with water. And they put the grass on top. And they put the camas. That's camas. They turn it back. And take it and... Mama used to put it in a gunnysack. And put it on there this way.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What do you mean, this way?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: This way. Stand like this. Like this thing.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Oh, the gunnysacks would stand up against each other?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah. Oh, I see. And it should burn itself. And it get ripe.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And then what do you do to eat it? To eat it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, we take it out. And we take it and dry it out. You can dry it out. Mama used to take the ones that are small. And she'd take that and pound it. To make soup out of it. It's your good soup. I've never eaten camas.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You never eat camas?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: You never eat cous?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How would you prepare cous?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, you have to dry it on a sun. My mama used to take it and put it on top of the house like this. Not just a cloth or something. Then put it on there. And dry it up. When it's dry it's good to eat.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Just like that?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: If you want to cook it, you can cook it. But if you want to eat it dry, it's dry.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How would you cook it if you wanted to cook it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Boil it. You can boil it and you can put a little grease or something in it. And it tastes good. Same with camas. Camas that's black. When they get ripe they turn black. They're black all the way through. So we take it. They used to take it and pound it. Some of it. They take it and they make it about this long.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: About a foot long or so?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: About this long. And dry it up like that. It used to be good to eat.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: When you were traveling along, would you eat dried meat and camas and things like that? How did you pull your teepees and things? How did you move all that stuff when you moved somewhere?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We used to take our teepee with us.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How? How would you do it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Pack it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: On a horse?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We used to go from here, clay to wallow. And then coming back we'd go up in the mountain. And that's where the boys used to hunt.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Up on Moscow Mountain there? What would they call Moscow Mountain?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: On this side of Wallowa. Oh! On this side of Wallowa. And we used to come clay down to Rapa when we get home. That's how we used to do it. We used to get salmon in Wallowa. Salmon, we used to get salmon. We used to take a dip nut and dip it with a dip nut.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you smoke the salmon or dry the salmon then too?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We just dry it. Not smoke it. Dry it. And it's good if you eat it dry, it's alright. If you cook it, it's alright. We used to eat eels too.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Eels? From where? Did you get them out of Wallowa Lake?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We used to get eels and we'd dry it just the same. But we have to have sticks to straighten them out so they can dry good. Just put it across like this. If it's in a fall time then we used to put fire on them. Mama used to do that. In the summer time you can dry it with the sun. It's good. I used to like it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How much time would you spend down in Wallowa each year? Wallowa? Where did you go?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: After July we'd go over there and stay over there about two weeks. Then we'd come back.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: In two weeks you managed to get enough fish and everything?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Oh, sure still. My grandfather used to get dip net. He'd dip it with a dip net. Salmon. We used to have dried salmon… yes.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How many people were there in those times? How many Nez Perce were there when you were making those big moves from Wallowa back to here? When you were still moving around? How big a tribe would be moving?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: There was lots of people who used to go to Wallowa.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would you all go in one bunch?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Or would you all go separately?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Some went up on the other side and some down. We used to go down all the time. We used to get salmon about this long. Those are big fish, a couple of feet long. We used to get... They used to even dry salmon. You can eat it dry, it's good. I don't have to cook it, but sometimes this backbone and the head... We didn't have no chief for that. We just used to go over there and camp.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you remember who any of the elders or the old people were?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Grandma, grandfather, and my grandmother.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What were their names?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Jonah Hayes, my grandfather's name was. And my grandmother's was Elizabeth.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: This was all after the war, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yes, it was after the war. After the war that they had.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What did the Nez Perce say about that war?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, I don't know. I don't know very much about it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were the Nez Perce sorry that it happened?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yes, they were sorry it happened that way. See, all kinds of... I don't know what they call it. Snake ..., I guess. They're the ones that used to come and fight the Nez Perce.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What would the fights be about?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, I don't know. Just try to take the land away from us. I think that's what it was. Take the land away.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: The Nez Perce were really good horsemen, weren't they?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yes… they were pretty good. They used to dry salmon, dry meat. Dry meat is awful good. Mama used to take it when we dried it and she'd take it and pound it. It'd be just purity.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Why would she pound it? Why would she pound it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, to make it better. When we had salt and she'd put a little salt on it when she started to dry it. And we'd have salt on it. That's what we used to do. That's why we used to go to Wallowa. That's why we used to go to Wallowa.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Were there some people who stayed all the time in Wallowa? Everybody had to come back to Lapwai?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No… nobody stayed there. The Oregon people would go in and us would go in too.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Didn't Chief Joseph want to stay there? Joseph?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: He was a horse. He was a... What do they call him? Chief… he was a chief.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Didn't he want to stay in Wallowa all the time?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No… we'd all go over and then we'd come back. When we got our land in Asotin. And that's where we'd be at. We stayed there. That's where I was born, in Asotin.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: In Asotin?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yes. His voice was born there too.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Is Asotin an Indian word?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Asotin.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What does it mean in this verse?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, that's Asotin. I don't know what that means. Asotin. That's Asotin. The white people call it Asotin. But Indians call it a Asotin. It's like Lapwai here too. I forgot what I was going to say. Did... He was a summertime. He used to go over there. Fresh. Different.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did you know Joseph? Chief Joseph?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh huh. He was close relative to us.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was he?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh huh. Yeah, he was close relative. But he stayed in the combat place now.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Over in Washington, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Uh huh. Yeah, he used to stay there. But when we all go to Waalau, we all be together.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would there be a big celebration then when you got there? Because the tribe was back together again?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No, nothing like that. They were just fish. They had dip nets to fish with.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would there be any dances or anything at that time? Or any marriages from the different tribes?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No. Nothing.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What was a Nez Perce marriage like in the early days?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, they used to just get married and they never get married at some place else. They just lived together, I think. That's what you want. Live together.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Wouldn't there be any sort of a ceremony where the tribe wouldn't know that those two people?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Just live together… they had trouble when they fought each other. But my father was white.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: How did he happen to come and marry a Nez Perce woman?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: We was living in Asotin. That's where they come.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Your mother was living in Asotin?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: This Asotin was Noe Penry's brother. My father was Noe Penry's brother.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Who Henry?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: He had Indian women. That's why my mother married her.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And your father's name was?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Len Henry. Len Henry.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: And what was his brother's name?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Noe Penry. Noe. He's living yet. He's just like this.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: He's old… living in the Southern African. That's where he's living. He's got kids and everything.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: That was your father's brother?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: That was my father's brother, Noe Penry.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was your father a trapper? How did he happen to come to this part of the country and marry your mother?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I don't know… i can't tell you that. I don't know how he came to marry. See, it was Noe Penry's brother. And he was staying with Noe Penry. That's where I was born.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Was Noe Penry an old fur trapper?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Noe Penry was my uncle. He was, but he's dead now.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Noe Henry is dead now?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: No, I think he's living yet. Oh yeah, they told me. He's getting so old he just walks out.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: All bent over?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: But my father died. His name was Land Henry. He died. My mama's name was Agnes Henry.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you have a Nez Perce name yourself? Me?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, my name is... I can't remember. It's kind of different. Oh, I can't remember it.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you remember what it means in English?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Nobody hardly calls me.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you remember what it means in English?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I don't know what it means. I don't know what it means.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would you like to sing me another song?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Ippinutso.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Ippinutso?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: That's what my name was.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Did your parents give you that name?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: My parents gave me that name. My grandfather. Jonah was my grandfather.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What is it again?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Ippinutso. Ippinutso.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know what it means in Nez Perce?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I don't know. Okay. I don't know.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you still speak much Nez Perce? Do you still speak very much Nez Perce?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, I speak Nez Perce.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: If you were to say hello to me, how would you say that in Nez Perce?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, in the afternoon it's Tats Avach. And in the morning it's Tats Meinmein. And in the evening it's Tats K'vareit. If they meet you in the morning they say Tats Meinmein. If they meet you in the afternoon, Tats Avach. If they meet you in the evening, Tats K'vareit.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What would I say back? Would I say the same thing back or would I say something different?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I don't know… i don't know if you'd tell them anything. Maybe you can… no, no.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: If I knew how to speak Nez Perce, what would I say back? Would I say the same thing?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: There's two of them. Two of you. You tell them Tats Meinmein. He'd say Tats Meinmein too. Tats Avach. That's afternoon. Good. May, May is morning. Now evening is K'vareit. Tats K'vareit. That's what you can say. If I tell you Tats K'vareit, you have to say the same thing. I see. Tats K'vareit.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Somebody coming in?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Yeah, they went back out again.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Would you like to sing me another song?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Of course.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What kind of song?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: Well, you sang me the one about He's Calling Us, and You Sang Me At The Cross.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know any others besides those two? At the Cross?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: You sang that one for me already. Yeah, I sang that.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know any other ones?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: I see… i can't remember the old songs. Okay.

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: Do you know any other hymns in Nez Perce? Not necessarily the old songs, but any of the Nez Perce hymns.

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: (sings)

segments.speaker: Rob Moore
segments.words: What does that mean?

segments.speaker: Alice Henry Jackson
segments.words: At the Cross, where we meet at the Cross, when there's an end of the world.
